# **Architectural Specification and Research Recommendations for Pair 4 Quantum Error-Correction Search Algorithms**

## **Executive Recommendation and Alternatives Considered**

The primary architectural recommendation for Pair 4's first functional prototype (Milestone 1\) is to implement a seeded, length-bounded, mutation-only evolutionary search engine alongside a uniform random-search baseline that evolves variable-length Clifford encoder sequences over the elementary gate set ![][image1]1. Rather than mutating binary check matrices directly, each candidate genotype in Pair 4 represents an ordered sequence of Clifford gate operations acting on ![][image2] physical qubits, which defines an ![][image3] stabilizer code by conjugating ![][image4] canonical single-qubit Pauli\-![][image5] stabilizers initialized on designated ancilla qubits2.  
This gate-sequence architecture resolves every correctness bug identified in the repository's existing research notes while strictly respecting the five-pair ownership boundaries. Because every Clifford gate ![][image6] is unitary and maps the ![][image2]\-qubit Pauli group ![][image7] to itself under conjugation (![][image8]), any sequence of such gates preserves both pairwise commutation (![][image9]) and algebraic independence over the binary field ![][image10]2. Consequently, every random initialization and every local gate mutation produces a valid ![][image3] stabilizer code with exact ![][image10] rank ![][image11], completely eliminating the invalid row mutations and real-valued rank errors (np.linalg.matrix\_rank over ![][image12]) present in the legacy notes without requiring Pair 4 to re-implement Pair 1's binary symplectic linear algebra5. Furthermore, evolving gate sequences aligns directly with Pair 2's mandate (Clifford circuit simulation and Pauli conjugation in Stim)7 and Pair 5's mandate (transformer modeling over tokenized gate sequences), whereas evolving check matrices would bypass both subsystems or require post-hoc circuit synthesis8.  
For Milestone 1, Pair 4 should restrict variation operators to bounded replace, insert, and delete gate mutations with balanced length-change probabilities (![][image13]) within hard length bounds ![][image14], explicitly deferring circuit crossover to Milestone 2\. Empirical findings in recent quantum error-correction evolutionary literature demonstrate that mutation-only evolutionary search (QDistEvol and custom stabilizer search in Webster and Browne, 2024\) avoids the destructive epistasis of crossover while achieving state-of-the-art code discovery9. Finally, because Pair 2's Stim wrapper and Pair 3's noise-aware evaluator are not yet implemented in the repository, Pair 4 should define a minimal, callable CodeEvaluator protocol returning a standardized EvaluationResult. This dependency-injection boundary allows Pair 4 to validate random sampling distributions, mutation invariants, seed reproducibility, and budget-matched search loops immediately using deterministic mock and surrogate evaluators.

### **Why Clifford Encoder Sequence Evolution Best Fits Pair 4's First Prototype**

While both paradigms guarantee algebraic validity, evolving ![][image26] encoder sequences is unequivocally superior for Pair 4's prototype within this project's collaborative architecture. First, it maintains strict compliance with subsystem ownership boundaries. Pair 1 owns binary symplectic math and stabilizer independence, Pair 2 owns Stim Clifford simulation and Pauli conjugation, and Pair 5 owns transformer gate tokenization. Implementing canonical check-matrix parameterization inside Pair 4 would require Pair 4 to construct symplectic standard-form matrices ![][image73], encroaching on Pair 1's domain10. Furthermore, canonical matrix evolution outputs a check matrix rather than a gate sequence, leaving Pair 2's Stim circuit simulator unused and depriving Pair 5's transformer of gate-sequence training trajectories unless an additional Gaussian circuit synthesis module (stim.Tableau.to\_circuit or Gottesman Section 4.2 synthesis) is interposed8.  
Second, evolving gate sequences directly synthesizes compact, hardware-executable encoding circuits. As noted in Webster and Browne (2024, Section II-A4, p. 3), interpreting canonical matrices ![][image63] and ![][image74] as circuits yields generic ![][image75] dense ![][image76] and ![][image77] networks9. By contrast, evolving bounded-length ![][image26] sequences directly discovers low-depth encoding circuits ![][image78] while allowing explicit parsimony pressure on gate count ![][image79] and circuit depth1. Third, the gate-sequence representation is surjective over all stabilizer codes: because every ![][image3] stabilizer code admits an encoding Clifford unitary ![][image80] that maps ![][image81] to its stabilizer generators (Gottesman, 1997, Section 4.2, pp. 33–41)4, and ![][image26] generates ![][image82] (including single-qubit Pauli gates via ![][image83] and ![][image84]), the search space of ![][image26] sequences covers the entire space of ![][image3] stabilizer codes18.

### **Assessment of Crossover: Why It Should Wait Until a Later Milestone**

Circuit crossover should be explicitly deferred to Milestone 2, leaving Pair 4's first prototype focused on mutation-only evolutionary search. This recommendation is grounded directly in the QEC evolutionary literature: in Webster and Browne (2024, https\://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.13017, p. 6), the authors explicitly note that their custom evolutionary algorithm for quantum error-correction code discovery and distance finding has no crossover and a low mutation rate9. Furthermore, in a Clifford sequence ![][image69], the action of the suffix ![][image241] on the stabilizer generators depends entirely on the intermediate Pauli frame created by the prefix ![][image242]. When one-point crossover concatenates Parent A's prefix with Parent B's suffix (Tandeitnik and Guerreiro, 2022, https\://arxiv.org/html/2210.05058v1, Section II, Fig. 3, p. 3\)1, Parent B's suffix acts on a completely foreign intermediate stabilizer tableau, behaving as a disruptive macro-mutation rather than preserving modular sub-circuits29. Finally, naive one-point crossover with independent cut points ![][image243] and ![][image244] produces offspring of length ![][image245] that frequently violate ![][image14], introducing truncation heuristics that confound baseline comparisons against random search.

## **Code Evaluation Metrics, Evaluator Interface Contract, and Pre-Evaluation Demonstrables**

### **Diagnosis of the Legacy Syndrome/Identity Metric**

The repository's existing evaluation notes score a candidate code by counting whether a Pauli error ![][image246] is the identity (![][image247]) or triggers a non-zero syndrome (![][image248]). This formulation is mathematically flawed for quantum error correction on two distinct counts. First, it fails to account for code degeneracy. In a degenerate stabilizer code—such as Shor's ![][image249] code, where weight-2 phase flips like ![][image250] belong to the stabilizer group ![][image122]—any non-identity stabilizer ![][image251] yields a zero syndrome (![][image252]) yet acts trivially as the logical identity on the codespace (![][image253]) and requires no recovery action (Webster and Browne, 2024, https\://arxiv.org/html/2409.13017v1, Section II-A5, p. 4\)9. Treating ![][image252] for ![][image251] as a failure falsely penalizes degenerate codes10. Second, the legacy metric conflates error detection with error correction. Triggering a non-zero syndrome (![][image248]) only indicates that an error is detected, not that it is uniquely correctable. For example, the ![][image254] code has distance ![][image255] and produces a non-zero syndrome for every weight-1 Pauli error13. However, distinct weight-1 errors share identical syndromes (e.g., ![][image256] while ![][image257] is a non-trivial logical operator), meaning no decoder can reliably correct weight-1 errors on a ![][image255] code. Scoring ![][image248] as success assigns a distance-2 error-detecting code the same perfect weight-1 score as the ![][image175] error-correcting code.

### **Distinguishing Distance, Harmful Undetected-Error Probability, and Decoder-Dependent Logical Failure**

Let ![][image117] be the stabilizer group, let ![][image258] be its normalizer (centralizer) in the Pauli group, and let ![][image259] be a memoryless Pauli noise model assigning probability ![][image260] to each unsigned ![][image2]\-qubit Pauli operator ![][image261] such that ![][image262] (Webster and Browne, 2024, https\://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.13017, Section II-B, Eq. 8, p. 4\)9. Every unsigned Pauli operator ![][image263] falls into one of three mutually exclusive algebraic sets: the ![][image41] harmless stabilizers ![][image264] that have zero syndrome (![][image252]) and act trivially on the logical space9; the ![][image265] harmful undetectable logical errors ![][image266] that also have zero syndrome (![][image252]) but enact a non-trivial logical transformation on the encoded information9; and the ![][image267] detectable errors ![][image268] that trigger a non-zero syndrome (![][image248]), whose successful correction depends on the decoder's recovery operator ![][image269]10.

The mathematical relationship among these three metrics has direct consequences for search landscape smoothness. If Pair 3 returns only integer distance ![][image162], Pair 4's evolutionary search will stall on flat plateaus because all random circuits with ![][image289] receive an identical score9. Conversely, if Pair 3 returns only ![][image275], search on an odd-qubit system may converge to a distance-2 code that detects weight-1 errors rather than a distance-3 code that corrects them. When Pair 3 builds its evaluator using its existing small-system error enumerator, the ideal scalar fitness returned to Pair 4 is either ![][image290] under an exact degenerate syndrome-coset lookup table (for ![][image291]), or a composite score combining ![][image292]9. Crucially, Pair 4 does not implement this error-correction math; Pair 4 simply maximizes the scalar fitness: float returned by Pair 3's evaluator contract1.

### **Minimal Evaluator Interface and Pre-Evaluation Demonstrables**

To decouple Pair 4 from Pair 2 and Pair 3's implementation timelines, Pair 4 should define a minimal structural typing contract (CodeEvaluator via typing.Protocol) within its own interface module. The protocol requires a single method evaluate(candidate: CircuitCandidate) \-\> EvaluationResult (along with an optional evaluate\_batch(candidates: Sequence\[CircuitCandidate\]) \-\> list\[EvaluationResult\] that defaults to sequential evaluation). Following the convention of Tandeitnik and Guerreiro (2022, Section II, p. 3\)1, Pair 4 strictly maximizes EvaluationResult.fitness (float), treating any candidate with is\_valid \== False or math.isnan(fitness) as having fitness \= \-math.inf.  
Before Pair 2's Stim conjugation module and Pair 3's noise evaluator are integrated, Pair 4 can demonstrate complete algorithmic and software readiness using three tiers of self-contained test doubles inside Pair 4's test suite. At the first tier (zero evaluator needed), Pair 4 can run statistical invariant suites over ![][image293] stochastic samples proving that two-stage gate sampling matches target probabilities ![][image294] within binomial confidence bounds, that ![][image77] never assigns ![][image295], that ![][image196] masks ![][image77] cleanly, and that 1,000 sequential mutations from ![][image213], ![][image296], and ![][image297] never violate ![][image14]. At the second tier, Pair 4 can inject a deterministic TargetCircuitSurrogateEvaluator that scores a CircuitCandidate using structural sequence similarity (such as negative Levenshtein edit distance or gate-pair n-gram overlap against a hidden target Clifford sequence), demonstrating that ![][image298] and ![][image299] selection, elitism, parsimony tie-breaking, and evaluation budget caps climb smooth and rugged landscapes reproducibly. At the third tier, Pair 4 can inject a FixtureLookupEvaluator that maps known canonical encoder sequences (such as the 2-gate ![][image300] bit-flip encoder) to optimal fitness scores and single-mutation neighbors to intermediate scores, verifying end-to-end ranking and trajectory export.

## **Benchmarking Methodology: Baselines, Fair Budgets, Validation Fixtures, and Epistemic Separation**

### **Why Evolutionary Search Must Not Be Assumed to Outperform Random Search**

A rigorous research prototype must treat the performance of evolutionary search relative to random search as a falsifiable empirical hypothesis rather than an axiom. In quantum circuit synthesis and QEC code discovery, the genotype-to-phenotype map from Clifford gate sequences to stabilizer codes is highly non-local and epistatic29. Inserting or replacing a single ![][image77] gate near the beginning of a circuit conjugates every subsequent gate, potentially jumping to an unrelated stabilizer code in ![][image52] and reducing the local autocorrelation of the fitness landscape. Furthermore, on small systems (![][image301]) or under coarse step-function metrics (such as integer distance ![][image162] without continuous ![][image278] or ![][image275] smoothing), evolutionary populations can prematurely converge onto a suboptimal ![][image255] local optimum while uniform Random Search (RandomSearch) continues sampling globally independent circuits and hits a ![][image302] encoder by chance. Conversely, Tandeitnik and Guerreiro (2022, https\://arxiv.org/html/2210.05058v1, Section IV, p. 11\) demonstrated that for the 7-qubit color code (![][image303]), a genetic algorithm achieved a ![][image304] success rate across runs within 10,000 generations whereas Random Search achieved ![][image305]1. Thus, whether evolution beats random search depends critically on ![][image306], the smoothness of Pair 3's fitness function, and the evaluation budget.

### **Recommended Baselines and Iso-Evaluation Budget Protocol**

Pair 4's prototype should implement three search algorithms under a unified SearchAlgorithm interface that terminates strictly when the number of calls to evaluator.evaluate() reaches a fixed budget ![][image307]. The architectural parameters and selection dynamics of these three baselines are contrasted in the table below.

| Search Baseline | Population Structure & Default Hyperparameters | Initialization Cost | Generation Variation & Selection Mechanism | Key Behavioral Role in Benchmarking |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Baseline 1: Uniform Random Search (RandomSearch)** | Memoryless independent sampling \+ 1 elite slot (best\_so\_far). | ![][image308] evaluation (first random draw). | At each step ![][image309], sample ![][image310] and draw ![][image79] random gates; update elite if (fitness, \-L) improves. | Null-hypothesis baseline testing whether local mutation provides any advantage over global blind sampling1. |
| **Baseline 2: ![][image311] Evolution Strategy (OnePlusLambdaES)** | 1 parent ![][image312], ![][image313] mutated offspring per generation, ![][image314] step per offspring. | ![][image308] evaluation (![][image312]). | Generate ![][image315] mutations of ![][image312]; replace ![][image316] if (C\*.fitness, \-len(C\*)) \>= (parent.fitness, \-len(parent)). | Minimal local-neighborhood climber; non-strict inequality (![][image317]) enables neutral drift across flat fitness plateaus. |
| **Baseline 3: ![][image318] Elitist EA (MuPlusLambdaEA)** | **![][image319]** elite parents, ![][image313] mutated offspring per generation, binary tournament size ![][image320], no crossover5. | ![][image319] evaluations. | Select ![][image315] parents via binary tournament; mutate each once; pool ![][image321], deduplicate identical gate tuples, and keep top ![][image322] unique elites5. | Maintains multi-lineage diversity to resist premature convergence on deceptive ![][image255] plateaus5. |

Two algorithmic details in OnePlusLambdaES and MuPlusLambdaEA are critical for stabilizer code search. First, in OnePlusLambdaES, the parent replacement rule must use non-strict lexicographic comparison (\>=) rather than strict improvement (\>), enabling neutral drift across iso-fitness plateaus so the climber does not freeze when single-gate mutations leave code distance unchanged. Second, in MuPlusLambdaEA, parent selection should use binary tournament selection (![][image320], Ghlib, 2026, https\://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13250053/, p. 8\)32 rather than fitness-proportionate roulette wheel selection. Binary tournament selection is invariant to positive affine transformations of the fitness metric, avoiding the numerical scaling instabilities that forced Tandeitnik and Guerreiro to multiply their fitness by an arbitrary weight ![][image323] (https\://arxiv.org/html/2210.05058v1, Section III/IV, p. 5\)1.  
To guarantee fair comparisons, every call to evaluator.evaluate() must increment the budget counter by exactly ![][image308], and algorithms must be compared at identical ![][image307] checkpoints (e.g., ![][image324]), truncating the final offspring batch if fewer than ![][image315] evaluations remain. If optional candidate memoization (caching evaluations by candidate.gates tuple key) is enabled, benchmarks must log both Total Circuit Evaluations (including cache hits) and Unique Evaluator Calls (excluding cache hits). Following evolutionary circuit optimization standards (Ghlib, 2026, https\://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13250053/, p. 8, which mandates ![][image325] independent seeds)32, every benchmark configuration must be executed across ![][image326] deterministic integer seeds (seeds \= \[1000 \+ i for i in range(20)\]), reporting the median, interquartile range (IQR: 25th–75th percentile), mean ![][image327] standard deviation, target-code discovery rate, and a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test ![][image328]\-value comparing the evolutionary baselines against RandomSearch.

Project governance must enforce a strict boundary between software correctness verification (which gates code merges in continuous integration) and empirical claims of search improvement (which are scientific findings). Deterministic software correctness checks verify that random gate sampling and mutations obey all domain, qubit-index, and length constraints; that fixed seeds reproduce bit-for-bit identical search histories; that elitist algorithms (OnePlusLambdaES, MuPlusLambdaEA) exhibit strictly non-decreasing best\_fitness trajectories across evaluations; and that the search loop halts at exactly ![][image307] evaluations. By contrast, a claim of search improvement requires demonstrating a statistically significant gain (![][image352] over ![][image326] runs at identical ![][image307]) in median fitness or target-code discovery rate over RandomSearch. If RandomSearch matches OnePlusLambdaES on a specific landscape, the software implementation remains completely valid; the benchmark outcome simply diagnoses landscape ruggedness or fitness plateauing.

Second, the team must decide pipeline orchestration ownership: whether Pair 3's CodeEvaluator implementation internally calls Pair 2 (to conjugate CircuitCandidate into Pauli strings) and Pair 1 (to obtain the binary check matrix ![][image33]), or whether a thin top-level coordinator composes Pair2.conjugate \-\> Pair1.to\_symplectic \-\> Pair3.score and passes that composed callable into Pair 4\. Third, Pair 3 must specify its primary Milestone 1 fitness formula—whether it will return exact degenerate logical failure rate ![][image278] via syndrome-coset enumeration over its small-system error enumerator, harmful undetected error rate ![][image275], or a composite score combining ![][image292]9. Fourth, Pair 5 must clarify whether its transformer training pipeline expects only the final elite circuits from each search run or the full chronological search trajectory \[(step, candidate, fitness), ...\] (including low-fitness early mutations) for offline reinforcement learning or decision-transformer conditioning.
